topic: Hydrogen-Donor Solvent Assisted Thermal Decomposition of Lignin
title: Hydrogen-Donor Solvent Assisted Thermal Decomposition of Lignin
authors_text: Alejandra Mart�nez Guajardo, Xianglan Bai, Kwang Ho Kim and Robert C. Brown
abstract: Lignin makes up ~30% of lignocellulosic biomass, one of the world’s most abundant renewable materials, and it is also separated in the wood pulping process while manufacturing paper. Phenols and benzenes can be produced from lignin by cracking, making it the source of valuable chemicals. When lignin decomposes into bio-oil, biochar and non-condensable gases, it generates free radicals that lead to secondary reactions and the formation of large molecular weight compounds. To address this problem, we hypothesized that a hydrogen-donor solvent assisted thermal decomposition of lignin at high temperature and pressure represents a possible pathway to avoid these reactive functional groups in bio-oil. Experiments were made in batch reactors using corn stover organosolv lignin as raw material and 2-propanol as a solvent varying the reaction times. The molecular weight distribution of the bio-oil recovered was analyzed using GPC (Gel permeation chromatography) and a compositional analysis was made by GC/MS (Gas chromatography/Mass spectrometry). These results were compared with experiments conducted in a sealed glass capsule micro reactor coupled with GC/MS. It was found that, during solvolysis, phenols with unsaturated C=C bonds on side chains react with hydrogen atoms from 2-propanol, and convert into short chain alkyl phenols. The yield of these compounds was increased with reaction time. These results were shown in the GC/MS analysis for both batch and micro reactors. The GPC results showed an increase in bio-oil compounds. Consequently, it is possible to say that thermal decomposition of lignin in hydrogen-donor solvent could produce bio-oil with a substantial amount of stable monomeric phenols.

topic: Sustainable Management of Algae in Eutrophic Ecosystems
title: Sustainable Management of Algae in Eutrophic Ecosystems
authors_text: William McNeary IV and Larry Erickson
abstract: The accelerated eutrophication of the world’s freshwater and marine ecosystems is a complex problem that results in decreased productivity, loss of biodiversity, and various economic woes. Controlling algae populations in a eutrophic water body has value in mitigating some of these negative effects. This project reviews a number of strategies for algae management, with a focus on sustainable practices that have minimal environmental impact. The information in the literature is then used to propose a design for an integrated algae-aquaculture system to be used for the dual purposes of nutrient assimilation and production of fish and algal biomass. Effectiveness of the proposed system and possible revenue streams to offset capital costs are examined; other solutions that utilize the techniques in the literature are also explored.

topic: Trash to Gas: Converting Space Waste into Useful Supply Products
title: Trash to Gas: Converting Space Waste into Useful Supply Products
authors_text: Alexandra Tsoras, Paul E. Hintze, Anne Caraccio, Stephen Anthony, Mononita Nur, Robert Devor and James Captain
abstract: The cost of sending mass into space with current propulsion technology is very expensive, making every item a crucial element of the space mission. It is essential that all materials be used to their fullest potential. Items like food, packaging, clothing, paper towels, gloves, etc. normally become trash and take up space after use. These waste materials are currently either burned up upon reentry in earth’s atmosphere or sent on cargo return vehicles back to earth: a very wasteful method. The purpose of this project was to utilize these materials and create useful products like water and methane gas, which is used for rocket fuel, to further supply a deep space mission. The system used was a thermal degradation reactor with the configuration of a down-draft gasifier to process the trash. The reactor was loaded with approximately 100g of trash simulant and heated with two external ceramic heaters with separate temperature control in order to create pyrolysis and gasification in one zone and incineration in a second zone simultaneously. Trash was loaded into the top half of the reactor to undergo pyrolysis while the downdraft gas experienced gasification to treat tars and maximize the production of carbon dioxide. Minor products included carbon monoxide, methane, and other hydrocarbons. The carbon dioxide produced can be sent to a Sabatier reactor to convert the gas into methane, which can be used as rocket propellant. In order to maximize the carbon dioxide and useful gases produced, and minimize the unwanted tars and leftover ashen material, multiple experiments were performed with altered parameters such as differing temperatures, flow rates, and location of inlet air flow. Multiple filters including cyclone filter, granulated activated carbon (GAC), and glass wool were implemented to strip the product gas of unwanted materials. A condenser was used to recover water in the outlet stream. Conversion was considered maximized when about 45g of water was recovered in the outlet reservoir, which was the total wet mass calculated from 100g of trash stimulant, and when about 5g of unreacted mass was leftover in the reactor, which was the total ash mass calculated. The condition that resulted in conversion closest to these requirements was heating at 600°C with a high flow rate of 10L/min split evenly between inlets at the top and bottom of the trash sample. According to the data received from these experiments, the process will be further scaled up and optimized to ultimately create a system that reduces trash buildup while at the same time providing enough useful gases to potentially fill a methane tank that could fuel a lunar ascent vehicle or other deep space mission.

topic: Carbon Management in the Post Cap-and-Trade Carbon Economy
title: Carbon Management in the Post Cap-and-Trade Carbon Economy
abstract: Carbon Management In the Post Cap-and-Trade Carbon Economy In this paper, we discuss an economic model for comprehensive carbon management that focuses on changes in carbon flux in the biosphere due to anthropogenic activity. The two unique features of the model include: 1. A shift in emphasis from primarily carbon emissions, toward changes in carbon flux, mainly carbon extraction, and 2. A carbon price vector (CPV) to express the value of changes in carbon flux. The CPV is multidimensional, including one key element that measures the anthropogenic changes in carbon sequestration, or carbon residence time. We introduce new concepts pertinent to the model, including Carbon Quality and Carbon Avidity, as elements of a broader construct that describes and defines the fundamentals of our economic model. The key focus with the economic model is the degree to which carbon flux changes due to anthropogenic activity. The economic model has three steps: 1. The CPV metric is used to value all forms of carbon associated with any anthropogenic activity. In this paper, the CPV used is a logarithmic chronological scale to gauge expected carbon residence (or sequestration) time. In future economic models, the CPV may be expanded to include other factors to value carbon. 2. Whenever carbon changes form (and CPV) due to anthropogenic activity, a carbon toll is assessed as determined by the change in the CPV. The standard monetary unit for carbon tolls is a carbon toll unit, or CTU. The CTUs multiplied by the quantity of carbon converted (QCC) provides the total carbon toll, or CT. For example, CT $ = (CTU $/mole carbon) x (QCC moles carbon). 3. Whenever embodied carbon (EC) attributable to a good or service moves via trade to a jurisdiction with a different CPV metric, a carbon toll (CT) is assessed representing the CPV difference between the two jurisdictions. This economic model has three clear advantages. 1. The carbon pricing and cost scheme uses existing and generally accepted accounting methodologies to ensure the veracity and verifiability of carbon management efforts with minimal effort and expense using standard, existing auditing protocols. Implementing this economic model will not require any new, special, unique, or additional training, tools, or systems for any entity to achieve their minimum carbon target goals within their jurisdictional framework. 2. Given the wide spectrum of carbon affinities across jurisdictions worldwide, the economic model recognizes and provides for flexible carbon pricing regimes, but does not undermine or penalize domestic carbon-consuming producers subject to imports from exporters in lower carbon pricing jurisdictions. Thus, the economic model avoids a key shortcoming of cap-and-trade carbon pricing, and eliminates any incentive to shift carbon consumption to jurisdictions with lower carbon tolls. 3. The economic model is a comprehensive, efficient, and effective strategy that allows for the implementation of a carbon pricing structure without the complete, explicit agreement of carbon consumers worldwide.

topic: Pyrolysis and Gasification of Sugarcane Bagasse
title: Pyrolysis and Gasification of Sugarcane Bagasse
authors_text: Yurancy Quinones, Akil Syed, Gautami Newalkar, Pradeep K. Agrawal, Carsten Sievers and Dr John Muzzy
abstract: Pyrolysis and Gasification of Sugarcane Bagasse Yurancy Quinones, Akil Syed, Gautami Newalkar, Pradeep Agrawal, Carsten Sievers, and John Muzzy School of Chemical & Biomolecular Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, Georgia 30332 A major advantage of biomass gasification is that any type of biomass can be converted to syngas, making it attractive for unmerchantable wood, harvest residue, and waste from the forest and paper industry. Biomass gasification can be considered as two processes in series – biomass pyrolysis and char gasification. The goals of this research are to investigate the viability of using sugarcane bagasse as a renewable energy source by investigating the effect of temperature, pressure, and heating rate on char morphology in order to find optimum pyrolysis conditions for best char gasification reactivity. Chars were obtained through pyrolysis in a PEFR (Pressurized entrained flow reactor) at pressures ranging between 5-20 atm and at temperatures between 600-1000 o C. Chars were tested for reactivity in CO 2 using TGA (Thermogravimetic analysis) and analyzed using XRD (X-ray Diffraction) and SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy) for char structure, and CO 2 and N 2 physisorption for char surface area. An atmospheric pressure tubular quartz reactor was built to partially gasify the PEFR-generated chars and to examine the evolution of char morphology and surface area at various stages of conversion. The residual chars were tested again using the same techniques as described above. At both low and high pressures, increasing pyrolysis temperature leads to reduced char reactivity, however, the decrease is more pronounced at higher pressures. At both high and low pressures, increased temperature leads to the formation of less mesopores and macropores. SEM images of both low pressure low heating rate chars and high pressure high heating rate chars show that as pressure and heating rate are increased biomass swells and becomes more spherical unlike its low pressure and/or low heating rate fibrous counterpart. Furthermore, the XRD peak intensities at 2θ angles of 22° and 44° increased at higher pyrolysis temperatures, suggesting the formation of inactive graphitic carbon.

title: Engineering Biochar: Preliminary Review
authors_text: Dakota Botts and Tom R. Marrero
abstract: The purpose of this study is to review the state-of-the-art uses of engineered biochar. In this review, published peer-reviewed articles from 2000 to date were retrieved. Information obtained indicates that engineered biochar can serve to control emissions of heavy metals and excess fertilizers; and for the better understanding of conditions to produce biochar. The materials and methods used to make biochar are significant factors towards potential applications. This preliminary review indicates that there are several applications for biochar that could be cost-effective and more sustainable than conventional means.

topic: Development of Low Cost Biodiesel Washing Process for Sub-Saharan Africa
title: Development of Low Cost Biodiesel Washing Process for Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Using vegetable oils to produce biodiesel is commonly carried out around the world. However, most techniques for producing biodiesel rely on sophisticated production methods that aren’t appropriate for rural or remote regions of developing countries. Tropical regions such as Cameroon in Central Africa are usually rich in biological resources, such as oil seeds. Most villages have limited resources so a low-tech appropriate technology based approach is required. This presentation will focus on solving a key challenge in the production of biodiesel from vegetable oil – removing the soap produced as a side product of the transesterification reaction – in a manner that is simple and cost effective for underdeveloped regions. The interfacial properties of soap and biodiesel are the basis of the wash method and additives. Evaluation of locally available resources for different wash additives with varying pH was conducted to yield the optimal washing process. The project described herein has been developed by the University of Kentucky Appropriate Technology and Sustainability (UKATS) Research Team in collaboration with the African Center for Renewable Energy and Sustainable Technology (ACREST), an NGO in Bangang, Village Cameroon. Further, the implementation of this process by a student team in Bangang Village, Cameroon in sub- Saharan Africa will be described. This project is part of a student led People, Prosperity and the Planet design project, sponsored by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Award No. SU835303

topic: University of British Columbia Biodiesel Project
title: University of British Columbia Biodiesel Project
abstract: UBC Biodiesel Project This is a proposal to submit a poster to the AIChE 2013 Student Conference poster competition, within the category of sustainability. It is our wish to present the UBC biodiesel project at the Sustainability Poster Competition as we feel that it is relevant to all three pillars of sustainability: Environmental, economic and social. In the poster we wish to present the technical details of this project as well as the sustainability goals outlined above, in the hopes of encouraging similar projects at other institutions. It would be an honour to present at the AIChe conference poster competition, as well as a fantastic experience to reward the work we have put in so far and become inspired by the other sustainability-oriented projects being presented. Torsten Søchting Jaccard t.jaccard@alumni.ubc.ca . University of British Columbia Abstract Biodiesel is a sustainable transportation fuel produced from vegetable oils or animal fats and can be used in any conventional diesel engine. Replacing conventional petro-diesel with biodiesel reduces CO 2 and other regulated emissions. The main goal of the UBC biodiesel project is to turn waste vegetable oil generated on campus into biodiesel. Instead of disposing this waste oil, the on-campus pilot plant turns it into a valuable product. UBC currently pays for disposal of waste vegetable oil, as well as paying for diesel fuel consumed by campus service vehicles. By closing the loop of waste-to-fuel on the UBC campus, the project ultimately improves UBC’s financial and sustainability. In addition to biodiesel, soap is also produced from the glycerine by-product and is used in labs throughout the department. This completes the loop of turning all of the waste-vegetable oil into useful products. The project, run exclusively by student volunteers from Chemical and Biological Engineering, utilizes a lab scale (70 L) biodiesel production facility. The plant is composed of two reaction vessels, one for esterification pre-treatment of waste oil and the other for the primary trans-esterification reaction, as well as an ion exchange column for dry washing of the biodiesel. In the fall of 2012, two 4 th year Engineering Physics students constructed a blend on demand pumping station as part of their senior project course. The system allows the user to fuel their vehicle with any desired blend of biodiesel, entering it on a control panel. With the support of the department, faculty and external funding, the project has sold over 800L of blended biodiesel fuel to UBC Housing and Hospitality Services for use in their delivery truck. This equates to CO 2 emissions reductions of 365 kg. The UBC biodiesel project is also a great educational experience for the undergraduate volunteers. The engineering departments can be daunting places for undergraduate students and standardized curriculums offer little opportunity for application of the knowledge gained in class. The UBC biodiesel project gives students this rare opportunity, through plant operation and fuel testing, which includes performing gas chromatography and cloud point measurements. The focus of many large universities is on research and interactions between undergraduate students and graduate students or professors are limited. The UBC biodiesel project pairs a graduate student with a group of undergrads in biodiesel production teams. This has yielded amazing results, with a number of undergrads working on the project for three years. It is a testament to the students involved as well as the mentorship of our graduate students that this project has not only continued, but expanded.

title: Sustainability Assessments in Developing Regions
authors_text: William Croft and Jeffrey R. Seay
abstract: Sustainability Assessments in Developing Regions William Croft & Jeffrey Seay University of Kentucky Current day society is facing the escalating issue of maintaining global equilibrium. Factors contributing to the equilibrium imbalance include: global warming, energy, population, the economy, etc. Sustainability has the ability to integrate the array of contributing factors making the application crucial to global equilibrium. The understanding and application of sustainability is gradually emerging, however, sustainability is often generalized and misconstrued. Sustainability assessments are commonly used in industry to promote a secure future while leaving a minimal footprint. Product and process designs can be assessed then sustainably optimized. Current assessments are applicable to most products and processes; however, assessment metrics are not adaptive to all global regions. Geography and impact have a direct relationship requiring the ability of an assessment to be calibrated for regional accuracy. In consequence, commonly used sustainability assessments are not effective in developing regions. Assessments for developing regions should encompass regionally appropriate economic, ecological and social indicators. Deployment of a sustainability assessment that accurately assesses developing regions can be transformative to regional and global equilibrium.

topic: Design, Fabrication, and Testing Of Multi-Component Absorption Columns Via 3-D Printing For Optimized Clean Energy Processes
title: Design, Fabrication, and Testing Of Multi-Component Absorption Columns Via 3-D Printing For Optimized Clean Energy Processes
authors_text: Christopher I, Hawkins and Jason E. Bara
abstract: Through 3-dimensional computer-aided design (CAD) programming, multi-component absorption column prototypes were designed, fabricated through 3-D printing, and tested to determine mass transfer rates via countercurrent carbon dioxide and solvent flow analyses. Modifications to the contactor trays and prototype components as well as overall part design were made in order to improve mass transfer. Thermodynamic and fluid modeling were also used on each design through computational flow simulations to determine optimal contactor design. Degradation analyses of the plastics used via scanning electron microscope (SEM) imaging were also performed to ensure part strength and durability. This process supports the notion that 3-D print designs can be utilized for commercial part design and testing purposes. This concept has the potential to save both time and money by using less valuable materials for initial testing and simulating flow through the parts computationally, rather than physically.

topic: Piperylene Sulfone: A Recyclable Substitute for Dimethyl Sulfoxide
title: Piperylene Sulfone: A Recyclable Substitute for Dimethyl Sulfoxide
authors_text: Afrah J. Boigny, Zachary J. Randall, Esteban E. Ure�a-Benavides, Charles Eckert and Charles L. Liotta
abstract: Piperylene sulfone is presented as a separable and recyclable dipolar, aprotic solvent substitute for dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). DMSO is a dipolar, aprotic solvent often used in industry for conducting chemical reactions. However, DMSO presents several challenges in terms of product isolation and separation. Its relatively high boiling point and product dependent separation leads to costly and inefficient recycling strategies. Piperylene sulfone has similar solvatochromic properties to DMSO but unlike DMSO, which has a melting point of 19 °C, piperylene sulfone has a melting point of -12 °C. At 110 °C, piperylene sulfone decomposes into 1,3-pentadiene and sulfur dioxide; these volatile compounds are captured and recombined to reform piperylene sulfone, which is the recycled to the reactor. For example, the nucleophilic substitution reaction of benzyl chloride and potassium thioacetate, to yield benzyl thiocetate, takes place in piperylene sulfone at comparable rates than in DMSO. The second order rate constants were greater than 1800 mL mol -1 s -1 . Once the reaction is complete, the reaction mixture is heated to 110 °C, where the solvent decomposes leaving only the product in the reactor. After recombination eighty-seven percent of the solvent was recovered. The built in recovery of this novel solvent enables for economically competitive and sustainable processes.

topic: A Comparative Life Cycle Assessment of Wild Algae Versus Petroleum
title: A Comparative Life Cycle Assessment of Wild Algae Versus Petroleum
abstract: Abstract: A Comparative Life Cycle Assessment of Wild Algae versus Petroleum Carbon dioxide is the primary greenhouse gas contributing to global climate change. Anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions have increased drastically since the start of the industrial revolution. This is a serious problem as the continued unsustainable use of “reduced carbon” from petroleum threatens the long-term health of the planet. Many development paths are being explored for replacing petroleum with biofuels for transportation. A proper life cycle assessment would enable the determination of whether a biofuel is a better alternative than the petroleum. I have performed a life cycle assessment (LCA) of macroalgae from Jamaica Bay New York and compared this to the use of petroleum to produce fuels. This LCA takes into account emissions due to algae farming and processing to a fuel that is a drop-in replacement for refined petroleum. The overall fuel that can be produced from this process is also discussed.
